"TOOK TO DRINK."
“IRRITATED” BY MISSING HIS BOAT.
FORGED LOST CHEQUES.
American Sent to Jail for Four Months.

That he took to drink "irritated" by missing his boat in Kobe and under its influence cashed cheques which he found in a pocket book lying on the wharf was the plan put forward by an American seaman at the Central Magistracy this morning when charged with forgery.

The accused, who passed under the name of Merjith H. Jones when arrested by the police at the Kowloon Hotel on Tuesday, was charged before Mr. H. R. Butters at the Central Magistracy the following day with being found in the Colony without a valid passport. This charge was only the forerunner of more serious charges. The accused later admitted that his proper name was Richard Edward Dunn.

At the proceedings this morning, there were three charges against the accused in respect of travellers' cheques issued by the American Express Company. The first was forgery of the cheques, the second cashing, them, and the last possession.
The accused pleaded guilty to all three charges and made a statement after the close of the evidence.

The only witness who was called upon to give evidence was Mr. Frank B. Dittman, purser of the s.s. President Cleveland. He stated that the accused, whose name was R. E. Dunn, worked as a night watchman on the vessel and skipped away at Kobe without proper discharge. Witness added that Mr. M. H. Jones was a passenger on his vessel bound for Manila and a report was made at Kobe that his pocket book containing travellers' cheques of the American Express. Company was missing

M. F. C. Vaux, appearing for the American Express Company, said that a report was made to the Company's Shanghai that several cheques issued in favour of Mr. Jones had been stolen or lost. The Company immediately circulated the news to their branches and other concerns. The sum involved in the missing cheques was gold $2,500, of which $1,600 worth of cheques had been found on the accused number had been negotiated, and $450 was still out and may be presented in due course, as Mr. Vaux said that the cheques went from hand to hand a long time like ordinary bank notes before they were presented at the Company's offices. As the American Express Company had taken years to build up the travellers' cheque business, and the loss of a cheque would be damaging to their reputation, Mr. Vaux asked His Worship to take a serious view of the case. He mentioned that Mr. Jones, who was now in Manila, was bringing a claim against the Company in respect of the missing cheques.

The accused made a statement in the course of which he said that he went ashore at Kobe and on coming to the wharf he found that the vessel had already left. Here he picked up a pocket book with the cheques made out in favour of Mr. Jones. Irritated by the fact that he missed the boat, he went and had some drinks and under its influence, commenced to cash the cheques, signing them as M. H. Jones. He added that he had borne a good character in America, and it was only the missing of the boat and the drinks which upset him.
At this stage the accused was sentenced to three months hard labour on the first two counts and one month on the last count, the sentences to run concurrently.

Considering that the American Express Company were faced with claims from various people, Mr. Vaux applied for the restitution of the property found on the accused. These comprised $246.50 in Hongkong currency, an Elgin watch, three gold rings, one gold and jade ring, one piece jade, one silver cigarette case, and some clothing. Mr. Vaux said that the method adopted by the accused was for him to give a cheque after buying a small article and then receive the balance in cash. The Russian colony in Berlin roads many possibilities into a dispatch sent to the "Berliner Tageblatt" from Moscow by Paul Scheffer, who declares that the future of Trotsky will be the real test of the success of the present comprehensive attempt of the Bolsheviks to conciliate the Russian penalty, that is to any, the vast bulk of the population. "He was," writes Scheffer, "the man who always advocated the regeneration of the party by infusion into it of the healthy, natural blood of the country. Over the head of the party, he is the attractive, fascinating, magic force. I believe that we shall see Trotsky again. His accommodation with the party would be the symbol of their accommodation with the country."

Several Chinese, and foreign detectives visited the house of Rue Amiral Bayle, the interior of which was found to be a kind of blacksmith's shop of three storeys. Here were found 31 miserable and half-starved boys between the ages of 12 and 15 years, many of them showing signs of scars and burns which are alleged to be the result of most brutal treatment. The owner of the premises, who proved to be a well-dressed and prosperous individual, was arrested together with a woman who was also found in the building. The apartments of Yu Pa-hong, were well furnished and amongst other property seized was found a stick with a gold band, a motor cycle and a camera, the latter being in excellent condition.

The Court found him guilty of drunkenness on board the s.s. Halvard on April 19 and 20 and suspended his certificate of competency for one year.
The second accused is a coolie and was arrested the next day on the China Merchants Wharf, French Bund. It was stated for the prosecution that he had confessed to having kidnapped many of the children whom, he said, he sold to the first accused for $5 a head. First accused also pleaded guilty.

It was alleged by the prosecution that all the children had been confined to the premises of the blacksmith's shop, which was well barred and bolted and none of them had been allowed to leave the premises during their captivity. One of them, the oldest, is alleged to have been confined to the premises for six years. These unfortunate children are said to have heed compelled to work day and night and to have received two scanty meals of rice a day. A pair of handcuffs were also found by the police suspended to one of the walls, which it is alleged were used as a punishment for anyone who refused to work, the unfortunate child being suspended by the wrists.

Inquiries have been made by the French Police in order to find the parents of the children and already two of them have been claimed, one by a Chinese resident in Rue Lafayette and the other by a resident in the Chinese City. The remainder were removed to the French Police Station, where they are awaiting other claimants. The appearance of these children is nothing short of pliable and their ragged clothes and scarred bodies reveal the hardship which they have suffered. Most of them are natives of Anhui and are apparently from quite humble homes.
It is also alleged that from time to time a number of the children have been sold to various purchasers for the nominal sum of $5 each. The premises show no signs of any sleeping accommodation and most of the children were apparently forced to seek their night's rest where best they could. Nor were they provided with any bedding during the winter. A medical examination showed one of them to be in a very bad condition.
The proceedings against the three accused were adjourned for further hearing.
